summary: Describes how the lightweight key exchange EDHOC can run over CoAP and be used by two peers to set up a security context for OSCORE. It specifies several additional details for this use, such as how messages are carried.

plainLanguage.summary: Two tiny gadgets need to agree on a secret handshake before whispering. This explains how they do that handshake using the small messages tiny gadgets use.

questions: how to run edhoc over coap
how does edhoc combined with oscore work
what is the coap edhoc option
how many round trips does edhoc oscore need
subtitle: How two tiny devices set up OSCORE keys with EDHOC over CoAP, and how to squeeze that into two round trips.

tldr.problem: Running the EDHOC key exchange and then the first OSCORE request one after the other takes three round trips, which hurts on slow radio links used by constrained devices.
tldr.mechanism: The client packs EDHOC message_3 and its first OSCORE-protected request into one CoAP message flagged with a new, empty EDHOC option (number 21), so the whole setup takes two round trips. The RFC also fixes how EDHOC connection identifiers are used with OSCORE and defines web-link attributes for discovering EDHOC resources.
tldr.outcome: The combined request cuts latency but only works for the forward message flow without message_4, and its benefit can be lost with Block-wise transfers. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9668 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, so it is the current definition of EDHOC combined with OSCORE over CoAP. It builds on RFC 9528.

sections.title: Why EDHOC Needs a CoAP Companion
sections.content:
EDHOC (Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Over COSE, RFC 9528) is a lightweight authenticated key exchange for constrained scenarios. Its messages can travel over the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252), and the result can be used to set up a Security Context for OSCORE (RFC 8613).

This document details that combination and adds several optional mechanisms. The headline one merges the EDHOC run with the first OSCORE transaction. That matters because the number of message exchanges can have a substantial impact on the latency of the first OSCORE request on certain radio technologies, for example when an Internet of Things (IoT) device is configured in a network for the first time.

The saving is possible because EDHOC message_3 can be made relatively small, leaving room for OSCORE-protected CoAP data within the target MTU sizes. The readers are expected to know CoAP, CBOR (RFC 8949), OSCORE and EDHOC.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny gadgets talk over slow connections, where every back-and-forth costs time. This document finds a way to do the secret handshake with fewer trips.

sections.title: The Sequential EDHOC Flow
sections.content:
EDHOC lets two peers agree on a secret in a mutually authenticated way and gets forward secrecy from ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys. The peer that sends message_1 is the Initiator; the other is the Responder. An optional message_4 gives the Initiator key confirmation, for example when the Responder has no protected application message to send.

Over CoAP, the client acts as Initiator and sends a POST to the EDHOC resource, by default at the Uri-Path /.well-known/edhoc. The payload is the CBOR simple value true (0xf5) followed by message_1, which includes the client's connection identifier C_I. The server answers with a 2.04 (Changed) response carrying message_2 and its identifier C_R. The client then POSTs C_R plus message_3 to the same resource.

Once the checks pass, both sides derive an OSCORE Security Context as defined in Appendix A.1 of RFC 9528. C_R becomes the client's OSCORE Sender ID, so it appears in the kid field of the OSCORE option. Run one after the other, EDHOC and then OSCORE take three round trips. The two peers must agree beforehand on an application profile that describes how they use EDHOC.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the gadgets finish their whole handshake, one message at a time, and only then send their first real message. That is three trips back and forth.

sections.title: The Combined EDHOC + OSCORE Request
sections.content:
After receiving message_2, the client already has everything it needs to derive the OSCORE Security Context, before it sends message_3. So it can send message_3 and its first OSCORE request together. This is only possible in the default forward message flow, where the client is the Initiator. With reversed roles it cannot be done.

The EDHOC + OSCORE request is a single CoAP message built as follows. C_R is not sent in the payload, because it is already the client's OSCORE Sender ID in the kid field of the OSCORE option. The payload is COMB_PAYLOAD = EDHOC_MSG_3 | OSCORE_PAYLOAD: message_3 is prepended to the OSCORE ciphertext. Message_3 goes in the payload rather than an option because it may be too large, for example with a long certificate chain or large External Authorization Data.

The message is flagged with the new EDHOC option. It is Critical, Safe-to-Forward and part of the Cache-Key, it MUST occur at most once and MUST be empty, and any value sent MUST be ignored by the recipient. It is used only in requests and is of Class U for OSCORE. Its option number is 21. The OSCORE ciphertext is not computed over message_3, which is not protected by OSCORE.

With the optimization, the minimum of two round trips is reached. Without it, that minimum cannot be achieved.
sections.plainLanguage: The first gadget notices it can already read the secret code after the second message. So it sends the last handshake piece and its first real message in one envelope, with a small flag saying that the envelope holds both.

sections.title: Client and Server Processing
sections.content:
The client composes message_3, establishes the new OSCORE Security Context and encrypts the original request with it, builds COMB_PAYLOAD, puts it in place of the OSCORE payload, adds the EDHOC option and sends the request. With the same server, the client SHOULD NOT have multiple simultaneous outstanding EDHOC + OSCORE requests that pertain to the same C_R.

The server MUST follow nine steps. It checks that the OSCORE option is present and the payload has the COMB_PAYLOAD format, otherwise it MUST reply 4.00 (Bad Request). It extracts message_3, takes the kid as C_R, finds the EDHOC session and processes message_3. If the application profile says message_4 shall be sent, the server MUST treat this as a client error. It then establishes the OSCORE Security Context, extracts the OSCORE ciphertext, rebuilds the plain OSCORE request without the EDHOC option, decrypts and verifies it, and delivers it to the application. An EDHOC option left in a decrypted request counts as an unprocessed critical option.

On success the server MUST reply with an OSCORE-protected response; message_4 does not apply. If EDHOC processing fails, the server aborts and answers with an EDHOC error message with error code 1, not protected by OSCORE and with Content-Format application/edhoc+cbor-seq, and it MUST NOT establish an OSCORE Security Context from that session.

With Block-wise transfers (RFC 7959), the client includes the EDHOC option only in the request carrying the first inner block. If COMB_PAYLOAD exceeds MAX_UNFRAGMENTED_SIZE, the client MUST abandon the Block-wise transfer and may fall back to the sequential flow. The performance advantage can be lost with specific parameter values and block sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving gadget opens the envelope, uses the handshake piece first to learn the secret code, and then uses the code to read the message. If the handshake piece is bad, it throws everything away and says so.

sections.title: Connection Identifiers and Application Profiles
sections.content:
The OSCORE Sender and Recipient IDs are the EDHOC connection identifiers, in both the sequential and the combined workflow. So the kid in the combined request is both the server's Recipient ID and C_R.

The Initiator MUST choose a C_I that is neither used in any current EDHOC session as its own identifier nor the Recipient ID in a current OSCORE Security Context where the ID Context is not present, and SHOULD NOT choose any current Recipient ID. The Responder follows the same rules for C_R and additionally MUST NOT pick a value equal to C_I. If the Initiator sees C_I equal to C_R in message_2, it MUST abort and reply with an EDHOC error message with error code 1. Following these rules lets each side omit the kid context in its OSCORE option.

For application profiles: a server that supports the combined request SHOULD say so explicitly in the profile of the resource. If a profile says the server shall send message_4, it MUST NOT claim support for the combined request, since that workflow is bound to fail.
sections.plainLanguage: Each gadget gets a name tag for the conversation. The rules make sure two conversations never wear the same tag, so mail never goes to the wrong place.

sections.title: Discovering EDHOC Resources with Web Links
sections.content:
Section 10.10 of RFC 9528 registers the resource type core.edhoc. This document adds target attributes so that a client can learn from a link (or filter a discovery request on) how a server's EDHOC resource is set up. A link that carries them MUST include rt=core.edhoc, and the values must be consistent with the application profile. Discovery can be done directly with the server or through a CoRE Resource Directory (RFC 9176).

  • ed-i and ed-r: the server supports the Initiator or Responder role. No value is allowed.
  • ed-method, ed-csuite, ed-cred-t, ed-idcred-t, ed-ead: a supported authentication method, cipher suite, credential type, credential identifier type, or External Authorization Data item. Each takes a single value and may repeat.
  • ed-comb-req: the server supports the EDHOC + OSCORE request. No value is allowed.

Because CoRE Link Format is weakly typed, string values that look like an integer MUST NOT be used in ed-idcred-t.
sections.plainLanguage: Before talking, a gadget can read a label on the door of another gadget that lists which secret handshakes it knows, so it only tries ones that will work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of OSCORE and EDHOC apply here as well. Sending several outstanding combined requests for the same session would not hurt security, because the server still processes a given message_3 only once and still enforces OSCORE replay protection.

With the combined flow, a minimum of 128-bit security against online brute-force attacks is reached once the client verifies the first OSCORE-protected response. As an example, with EDHOC method 3 and cipher suite 2, each side combines the 64-bit MAC in an EDHOC message with the 64-bit MAC in the AEAD of the first OSCORE message, giving 128-bit security for both the Initiator and the Responder.

Finishing EDHOC does not authorize the request. The rebuilt OSCORE request MUST undergo the same access-control checks as an individually sent one, so validated authorization information, such as an access token, has to be available before processing it.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening the door with the right handshake does not mean you may go into every room. The guard still checks your permission for each one.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered CoAP option number 21 with the name EDHOC. It also registered the eight attributes ed-i, ed-r, ed-method, ed-csuite, ed-cred-t, ed-idcred-t, ed-ead and ed-comb-req in the Target Attributes registry.

A new "EDHOC Authentication Credential Types" registry holds integer values with three initial entries: 0 for a CBOR Web Token (RFC 8392) containing a COSE_Key, 1 for a CWT Claims Set containing a COSE_Key, and 2 for an X.509 certificate (RFC 5280). Values from -24 to 23 need Standards Action with Expert Review, values from -65536 to -25 and 24 to 65535 need Specification Required, and values beyond that are Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers gets a new entry, number 21, so everyone agrees what the flag means. A new list is started for the kinds of ID cards a gadget can show.
